zamioculcas: Bright indirect light is best, and it also grows in partial shade or deeper in the room. Only morning sun is safe; midday rays scorch the glossy leaves.
Ordinary room air, 30–60 %, is enough. No misting — just wipe dust off the leaves now and then.
Comfort is 18–26 °C. In winter keep it above 15 °C, away from icy glass and draughts.
The tubers store water, so overwatering is worse than drought. Let the soil dry out completely between waterings.
Water only after the soil is fully dry — wet tubers rot
Use a pot with drainage holes and a loose succulent mix
Feed once a month in spring and summer, at half strength
Repot every 2–3 years, when the tubers fill the pot
The sap is toxic — wear gloves and keep it away from pets
dracaena: Bright indirect light by an east or west window. Variegated forms need more light; green ones accept light shade. Midday sun dries and fades the leaves.
Best at 40–60 %. Dry radiator air browns the tips: mist a couple of times a week or give a warm shower.
Keep 18–25 °C all year. Cold draughts and anything under 15 °C make the leaves droop and dry.
Brown tips come from dry air and chlorinated water. Use water that has stood.
Water with room-temperature water that has stood — chlorine and fluoride brown the tips
Let the top 2–3 cm of soil dry between waterings
Wipe dust off the leaves with a damp cloth
Feed every 2 weeks from spring to autumn
A bare cane can be cut — it will sprout from the sides
ficus: The brightest spot without long midday sun, ideally an east window. In dim light the leaves shrink and drop, and variegated kinds lose their pattern.
It likes 50–70 %: mist with soft water and give a warm shower once a month. Dry winter air is a common cause of leaf drop.
A steady 20–25 °C, with no swings. Draughts, a cold sill and air-conditioning all stress it.
It hates being moved and hates draughts — stress makes it drop leaves. Give it a permanent place.
Choose one spot — moving or turning the pot makes it shed leaves
Water moderately once the top 2–3 cm are dry
A shaping cut in spring makes the crown denser
Feed every 2 weeks while it is growing
The milky sap irritates skin — prune with gloves
calathea: Partial shade or soft light from a north or east window. Direct sun burns the pink pattern; deep shade fades it.
A tropical plant: 60–85 %. A humidifier or a tray of wet pebbles works best. Mist the air around it, not the velvety leaves.
A steady 20–24 °C all year. A cold sill and draughts make the leaves curl.
A fussy one: only soft, warm water. It lifts its leaves at night — that is normal.
Water only with soft warm water — hard water dries the leaf edges
Keep the soil evenly just moist, never a swamp
Leaves rise at night — that is a healthy movement
Feed every 2 weeks at half strength in spring and summer
Repot yearly into a loose, slightly acid mix
anthurium: Bright indirect light, no direct rays — sun dulls and burns the quilted leaves. A grow light helps in winter.
It wants 70 % or more, like a rainforest — a humidifier is almost required. Mist the air nearby and wipe the leaves.
Warm all year: 22–27 °C, not below 18 °C in winter. A sudden chill and draughts stop growth.
Grown for its quilted leaves. The mix must be airy; the roots need air.
A very loose, airy mix of bark, perlite and peat — roots need air
Water after the top dries, with no water sitting in the saucer
Once a month, a warm shower stands in for a tropical rain
Feed an aroid fertiliser every 2–3 weeks
Repot gently: the roots are brittle
caladium: Bright indirect light makes the red colour richest. Direct sun burns the thin leaves; deep shade turns them green.
Thin leaves dry fast — keep 60–85 % with a humidifier or a tray of wet clay pebbles. Mist the air: drops on the leaves leave spots.
While it grows, 21–27 °C; below 18 °C growth stops. The tuber winters warm, not under 16 °C, in almost dry soil.
In autumn it rests: the leaves die back and the tuber is kept almost dry until spring. That is not a disease.
In the growing season water often, but never leave it standing in water
In autumn the leaves die — that is dormancy, not death: cut watering to a minimum
Keep the tuber dry and warm in winter, then pot it again in spring
Feed every 2 weeks while it is growing strongly
The sap is toxic — handle the tuber with gloves
narcissus: Bright indirect light on a cool sill — an east or north window. While it flowers, light shade from direct sun makes the blooms last longer.
Ordinary 40–70 % is fine. Do not mist, especially the flowers: drops spot the petals.
The cooler it is, the longer it flowers: 10–18 °C is ideal. In a hot room the blooms fade in days. Keep it off the radiator.
A bulb with a clear rest. After flowering the leaves die back — that is normal. Cool air lengthens the bloom.
Water at the rim, not onto the bulb — water in the neck rots it
Keep the soil evenly moist while it grows and flowers
Cut the spent stem, but let the leaves die naturally — they feed the bulb
After the leaves die, store the bulb somewhere dry and cool
Bulbs and leaves are toxic — keep them from children and pets
chlorophytum-lemon: Bright indirect light by an east or west window gives the richest lime colour. It accepts partial shade, but deep shade makes the leaves pale and leggy. Midday sun leaves dry burn spots.
Undemanding: 40–60 % is plenty. In summer and when the heating is on, an occasional mist or warm shower also washes off dust.
Comfort is 18–24 °C. It can take a short drop to 10–12 °C, but that is a risk. In summer it can go to a balcony out of direct sun.
The Lemon form: a compact rosette of solid lime leaves, with no stripes. One of the easiest air-cleaning plants.
Water after the top 2–3 cm dry — thick roots store water, so overwatering is the danger
Dry tips mean dry air or chlorinated water: let the water stand
Feed a foliage fertiliser every 2 weeks from spring to autumn
Repot every spring — the roots fill and even crack the pot
Not toxic, and safe for pets, though cats like to chew the leaves
nephrolepis: Bright, diffused light near an east- or north-facing window — direct sunlight dries out and discolors the delicate fronds. It tolerates partial shade, but in deep shade, growth slows down, and the bush becomes sparser.
Tropical fern: comfortable at 60–90%. Mist the fronds daily or keep a humidifier nearby — in dry air, the tips instantly turn brown and fall off.
Comfort — 16–24 °C. It cannot tolerate temperatures above 26 °C near a radiator or below 12 °C — the fronds turn yellow and fall off.
A lush bush with feathery fronds responds well to a warm shower, but cannot tolerate dry air from radiators and air conditioners.
Keep the soil constantly slightly moist — complete drying out of the root ball is more dangerous than for most plants.
Spray the fronds daily or use a humidifier — dry air immediately dries the leaf tips.
Keep away from radiators and direct drafts, but ensure a supply of fresh air.
Fertilize every 2 weeks with half the dose of fertilizer for ornamental foliage plants in spring and summer.
One of the few ferns that are safe for cats and dogs — you don't have to worry about your pets.
adenium: It needs the sunniest spot in the house — a south-facing window and as much direct sunlight as possible. If there is not enough light, the stem will stretch, and you may not see any flowers.
A desert plant: dry indoor air with 20–50% humidity is quite comfortable. Misting is not necessary and is even undesirable — moisture on the caudex can cause rot.
Loves warmth: 20–30 °C year-round. In winter, when temperatures drop below 15 °C and the days are short, it enters a dry dormancy period.
A caudiciform desert plant: its thick stem stores water. When there is plenty of sunshine, it blooms with large pink flowers.
Water only after the soil has completely dried out — the thick caudex trunk stores water, and overwatering leads to rot.
Maximum direct sunlight: it blooms more readily on a south-facing window; in the shade, it stretches and does not bloom.
Loose soil with a high proportion of perlite or coarse sand and mandatory drainage
In winter, when it gets cold and the days are short, provide a dry dormancy period — almost without watering.
All parts of the plant are poisonous — the milky sap is dangerous if it comes into contact with the skin and mucous membranes.
monstera: Bright indirect light at an east or west window. In partial shade it still grows, but fenestrations are fewer and smaller. Direct midday sun leaves pale burns on the broad blades.
Comfortable at 50–70 %. In heating season, misting and wiping the leaves helps — dust blocks breathing and dulls the gloss.
A steady 18–27 °C. Below 15 °C growth stops; a cold draught blackens the edges of young leaves.
Leaf splits appear on a mature plant with enough light. Guide aerial roots into the soil rather than cutting them all off.
Water when the top 3–4 cm of soil are dry, and empty the saucer
Give a support — moss pole or trellis; aerial roots cling and leaves grow larger
You can rotate the pot, but do not move it every week
Feed every 2 weeks from spring to autumn with a foliage fertiliser
Sap irritates skin and is toxic to cats and dogs — prune with gloves
pothos: Bright indirect light keeps yellow and white variegation vivid. In partial shade it greens up but lives calmly even deep in the room. Direct sun bleaches the variegation.
Ordinary 40–60 % is enough. Dry air is not fatal, but tips brown less if you occasionally mist or wipe the leaves.
Comfort is 18–26 °C. Below 15 °C leaves yellow and drop; winter cold sills are best insulated.
One of the toughest trailing plants. Dull leaves after drought usually revive after watering if the roots have not rotted.
Water after the top 2–3 cm dry — fleshy stems store some water
Long trails can be trimmed; cuttings root easily in water
Yellow leaves at the base are more often overwatering than hunger
Feed every 2–3 weeks in spring and summer
Toxic to cats and dogs — keep trailing stems out of reach
aloe: It needs bright light and several hours of direct sun — a south or west window. In shade the rosette stretches, leaves thin and lie flat.
Dry air 30–50 % is its native environment. Do not mist: water in the rosette stagnates and rots.
Summer 18–27 °C; winter is better cooler, around 14–18 °C, with almost no watering. Below 10 °C leaves turn watery.
A succulent that stores water in its leaves. The main enemy is frequent watering and water sitting in the centre of the rosette.
Water rarely, only when the soil is fully dry — better to under-water
A tight pot, succulent mix and drainage holes are essential
On a cool winter windowsill, water once every 3–4 weeks
Pups at the base can be potted when they have their own roots
Do not take sap internally without medical advice — toxic to pets
sansevieria: It tolerates bright sun and fairly deep shade. In light, variegated stripes are brighter and growth is faster; in shade colouring greens but the plant survives.
Indifferent to humidity: 30–50 % and dry radiator air are fine. Wiping dust off the leaves is enough.
Comfort is 18–27 °C. It can take brief cool spells, but below 12 °C roots and leaf bases rot.
Nearly unkillable unless you overwater. Soft wrinkled leaves are usually rot from water, not thirst.
Water after the soil dries fully; even less in winter
Do not pour into the rosette centre or leave water in the saucer
A tight pot is even helpful — in a large one it barely produces offsets
Feed once a month in spring and summer at half strength for succulents
Sap irritates mucous membranes; toxic to cats and dogs
philodendron: Bright indirect light without direct rays. Green kinds live in partial shade; variegated ones lose pale sectors. Midday sun scorches thin young leaves.
It likes 50–70 %. Dry air does not kill at once, but new leaves emerge smaller with dry edges — a humidifier or pebble tray helps.
A steady 18–26 °C. Cold draughts and temperatures below 15 °C stop growth and blacken edges.
A relative of monstera. Do not cut off all aerial roots: they take moisture from the air and grip supports.
Water when the top layer is dry, with no soggy pot
Give climbers a support; leaves grow larger on a moss pole
Shorten long vines boldly in spring — the bush fills in
Feed every 2 weeks in the growing season
Sap is toxic to people and animals — keep away from cats
begonia: Bright indirect light at an east window shows off leaf patterns. Direct sun bleaches spots and dries edges; deep shade makes a loose, weak plant.
Needs 50–70 %, but velvet leaves dislike droplets: humidify the air around them, not the blades. Wet leaves in cool air spot easily.
Comfort is 18–24 °C. Below 15 °C and cold draughts drop leaves and buds.
Foliage and wax begonias fear overwatering more than a short drought. Turn the pot toward the light weekly so it does not lean.
Water at the pot edge when the top centimetre is dry
Do not leave water in the saucer more than half an hour
Remove spent flowers and yellow leaves so they do not rot
Feed a weak solution every 2 weeks while growing and blooming
A snug pot and loose perlite-rich mix protect tubers and roots from stagnation
orchid: Phalaenopsis needs bright indirect light: east window or west with a sheer curtain. Dark green leaves without a burgundy flush mean too little light; yellow patches mean burn.
Comfortable at 50–70 %. A tray of wet clay pebbles under the pot works better than misting the crown — water in the leaf axils rots.
Daytime 22–27 °C; a night drop to 18–20 °C helps set a spike. Below 15 °C roots stop.
Roots must see light and dry between waterings. Wrinkled leaves can mean drought or rotted roots — check inside the pot first.
Water by soaking bark 10–15 minutes when roots turn silvery
Clear pot with holes and bark, not ordinary soil
After bloom, trim the spike above a live node or at the base if it is dead
Orchid fertiliser every 2 weeks while growing; less in rest
Do not stand in water "up to the neck" or flood the rosette centre
cactus-barrel: Echinocactus needs direct sun several hours a day, ideally a south window. In shade the globe stretches, loses ribs and barely grows.
Dry air 20–40 % suits it. Misting is unnecessary and risky in cool weather: droplets on areoles rot.
Summer tolerates 25–30 °C by the glass. Winter is better at 10–15 °C with almost dry soil — that sets buds. Do not go below 5 °C.
It grows slowly and likes a tight pot. A soft base is almost always rot from excess water, not thirst.
Water only when soil is fully dry; in winter symbolically once a month
Mineral mix: sand, fine gravel, a little leaf mould, and drainage
After purchase, acclimate to sun gradually or you get white burns
Cactus fertiliser once a month only in spring and summer
Repot rarely and in gloves: spines sit deep
cactus-opuntia: Opuntia needs maximum direct sun. On a north window pads stretch, pale and break off easily.
Dry room air is familiar. Do not mist: moisture on pads in cool weather causes spots.
Summer 20–30 °C; it can go on a balcony. Winter benefits from cool 8–15 °C with almost no water. It does not tolerate frost in a pot.
Prickly pear propagates easily from "ears". Main needs are sun and sparse watering, or the base blackens.
Water after full drying; keep almost dry in winter
Light mix with sand and stone, pot with holes
New pads appear in spring — do not rotate the pot every week
A broken pad dries a couple of days and roots in dry sand

lavender: Lavender needs the sunniest spot: south window and at least 6 hours of direct light. In shade shoots stretch, grey and barely smell.

Comfort is 15–25 °C and fresh air. Winter room heat is too hot: cool 5–15 °C on a bright window is ideal. Heat above 28 °C without ventilation exhausts it.

Water when soil is dry several centimetres deep; do not keep the saucer wet
Lean, drained mix: soil, sand and a little lime, no heavy peat
After bloom trim spent spikes; in spring shorten the bush by a third
Feed lightly once a month, not excess nitrogen — else leaves, not flowers
Indoors, place near an openable window: without air movement the bush stagnates
basil: Basil needs lots of light: south or east window, supplementary light in winter. In shade stems stretch, leaves shrink and lose scent.
Ordinary 40–60 % is fine. Do not mist a dense bush — wet leaves mould easily in a warm room.
Warm 18–26 °C and no cold windowsill. Below 15 °C it stops; draughts blacken leaves.
Pick leaves from the top, not by stripping the base. Cold tap water and wet roots are a common cause of black stems.
Keep soil evenly moist but not flooded — water must drain from the saucer
Pinch tops once there are 4–6 leaf pairs — the bush branches and blooms later
Cut flower spikes: after bloom leaves toughen
Resow every few months: in a pot this is short-lived greens, not a tree
mint: Bright indirect light or soft morning sun. Harsh midday sun on south glass wilts leaves; deep shade makes them sparse and weak-flavoured.
It likes fresh air and 40–70 %. Dry radiator heat dries edges — keep it away from the heater.
Cool suits it better than heat: 16–24 °C. Above 28 °C in a closed room the plant wilts even in wet soil.
Mint drinks more than most herbs. If leaves droop, first check whether the root ball dried out before blaming disease.
Water often so soil never fully dries, but do not stand the pot in water
Plant in its own pot: roots quickly take over all the soil
Harvest shoots regularly — that is crop and keeps it from flowering
Renew by division each season: the old centre goes bare
Feed moderately, or you get watery growth without aroma
rosemary: Rosemary needs direct sun several hours a day. In shade shoots are thin, bare below and barely aromatic.
Dry air 30–50 % beats humid. In a damp, stale kitchen needles mildew.
Summer 18–25 °C with airflow. In a warm winter room it declines: better 8–15 °C on a bright window and sparse watering.
A Mediterranean shrub. In pots it is more often killed by overwatering than drought — roots must breathe.
Water when the top few centimetres are dry — standing water kills roots faster than drought
Sandy, stony mix and a pot with good drainage
Cut young shoot tips; do not cut old wood back to bare trunk
Do not mist a dense crown in the evening
Rare, weak feeding in spring and early summer
tulip: Forced bulbs need bright light and cool conditions. Direct sun on hot glass shortens bloom; a dark room stretches flower stems.
Ordinary 40–60 % is enough. Do not mist flowers — petals spot and stick.
Cooler means longer vase life in the pot: 10–16 °C is ideal. At 22 °C and above flowers last only days. At night it can go to a glazed balcony without frost.
A potted tulip is forced flowering for a short show. Rest after leaves fade is normal: dry the bulb and keep cool until replanting.
While growing and blooming, keep soil moist but do not flood the bulb
After bloom cut only the flower; leave leaves until yellow
Water at the rim, not into the bulb centre
In a warm room move away from the radiator the day it opens
Bulbs are toxic to people and animals — do not leave them in sight after digging up
violet: African violets need bright indirect light 10–12 hours, best east window or a lamp. Direct sun scorches velvet leaves; shade stops bloom and stretches petioles.
Comfortable around 50–60 %. Do not pour or spray water on leaves: drops spot and a wet crown rots.
A steady 18–24 °C. Cold windowsill and draught chill roots; heat above 27 °C dries buds.
It blooms almost year-round with enough light and a snug pot. Long petioles and no buds almost always mean too little light.
Water via saucer or at the rim with warm water when the top layer is dry
Small pot: in a large one it grows leaves and does not flower
Remove old lower leaves; do not bury the crown when repotting
Violet fertiliser weak every 2 weeks while budding
Brush off dust; do not rub leaves with a wet cloth
peperomia: Bright indirect light keeps variegated leaves sharp. It accepts partial shade; direct midday sun leaves dry spots on fleshy blades.
Ordinary 40–60 % is enough. Thick leaves hold moisture; mist rarely and only the air, not puddles on leaves.
Comfort is 18–25 °C. Below 15 °C on a cold window growth stops and leaves drop.
A compact plant with water stored in leaves. It suffers more from caring too much with water than from forgetting.
Water after the top 2–3 cm dry — overwatering rots fine roots
Small pot, loose mix with perlite
Do not place against a radiator: leaf edges dry
Feed once a month at half strength in spring and summer
Leaf or stem cuttings root easily in warm soil
hoya: Hoya needs bright light with direct morning or evening sun. In shade vines grow but no flower stalks form. Midday heat on south glass is best softened with a curtain.
40–60 % is plenty. Fleshy leaves do not need constant misting, though a warm shower for dust is welcome.
18–26 °C year-round. Winter can be slightly cooler, around 16 °C, with less watering. Below 12 °C leaves yellow and drop.
It blooms on old growth. Years without umbels usually mean too little light, not fertiliser.
Let soil dry between waterings — hoya is closer to succulents than vines
Do not cut short bare peduncles: buds return on them
Do not move or turn the pot when buds form — it drops them
Flowering fertiliser every 3 weeks in spring and summer
Tight pot and support or hanging: long vines dislike frequent repotting
bromeliad: Guzmania needs bright indirect light. Direct sun bleaches the bract; deep shade greens the rosette and fades colour.
It likes 50–70 % and fresh air. Dry radiator heat dries leaf tips faster than under-watering the cup.
Warm 18–27 °C without cold draughts. Below 15 °C the rosette stalls and cup water rots easily.
An epiphyte: it drinks mainly from the cup, not roots. After the bract fades the plant is not "broken" — it leaves pups.
Keep a little soft water in the central cup; change it every 1–2 weeks
Water the mix moderately: roots are weak and rot in swamp
The bright "flower" is bracts — they last months, then the mother rosette slowly declines
Pups at the base can be separated when one-third the mother’s size
Very weak feed into the cup, once a month in the growing season
spathiphyllum: Peace lily does well in partial shade and soft diffused light. Direct sun yellows leaves; a very dark corner stops flowering.
It likes 50–70 %. Dry air dries tips: misting and a pebble tray help, especially in winter.
A steady 18–25 °C. Cold draught and below 15 °C blacken edges and make leaves droop.
Drooping leaves almost always mean a dry root ball, not temperament. Black tips are more often dry air or stagnant water.
Water when the top layer is dry; drooping leaves are the first sign of thirst — they usually rise after watering
Do not let it wilt often: that dries tips
Wipe broad leaves free of dust
Flowering fertiliser every 2 weeks from spring to autumn
Cut spent spathes at the base so the plant does not spend energy on seed
dieffenbachia: Bright indirect light keeps leaf spots clear. In shade pattern greens; direct sun leaves dry patches.
Comfortable at 50–70 %. Dry air and radiators dry wide leaf edges — showers and wiping help.
Warm 18–26 °C without draughts. Below 15 °C it drops lower leaves; a cold window can rot the stem.
Lower leaves drop over time — that is stem growth, not always disease. Watch that the drop is not sudden and massive.
Water after the top 2–3 cm dry; less in winter
Rotate the pot so the stem does not lean to the window
A bare stem can be shortened: the top roots, the stump sprouts sides
Feed every 2 weeks in the growing season
Sap burns skin and mouth, dangerous to children and pets — cut in gloves
aglaonema: Green aglaonemas live in partial shade; pink and red need brighter indirect light or colour dulls. Direct sun scorches leaves.
Best at 50–70 %. Dry air dries edges, but it is more patient than calathea. Wipe leaves and keep off radiators.
Warm 18–26 °C year-round. Cold below 16 °C and draughts leave grey wet patches.
One of the few brightly coloured plants that honestly grows away from the glass. Slow but without daily fuss.
Water when the top layer is dry; do not leave water in the saucer long
Give variegated kinds a brighter spot than green ones
Wipe dust with a damp cloth — otherwise colour looks dirty
Feed every 3 weeks in spring and summer
Sap irritates skin and is dangerous to pets
tradescantia: Variegated tradescantias need bright indirect light or stripes green. Direct midday sun fades leaves; green kinds accept partial shade.
Ordinary 40–60 % is enough. In dry air tips brown, but the plant renews easily with pruning.
Comfort is 16–25 °C. Below 12 °C vines wilt; a hot radiator dries and shrinks leaves.
Fast trailing greenery. If the base is bare, that is not final: cut tips and plant them back in the same pot.
Water after light drying of the top layer — constant damp rots stems at the base
Pinch tips regularly so vines do not go bare
Renew an old stretched plant with cuttings — they root in water in a week
Feed every 2 weeks in the growing season
Sap may irritate skin; not ideal for cats
maranta: Maranta needs soft diffused light or partial shade. Direct sun bleaches pattern; deep dark makes a loose, pale plant.
Tropical: 60–80 %. Dry air rolls leaves into tubes. A humidifier beats frequent drops on velvet blades.
A steady 18–25 °C. Cold windowsill and draught stop growth; below 15 °C leaves wilt.
The "prayer plant" folds leaves at night. Leaves curled by day usually mean dry air or a dried root ball.
Keep soil slightly moist with soft warm water, never swampy
It raises leaves in the evening — normal movement, not disease
Keep away from radiator and air conditioner
Feed at half strength every 2 weeks in spring and summer
Divide when repotting; roots dislike drying out
strelitzia: Bird of paradise needs lots of bright light and several hours of direct sun, or it will not bloom and only grows a leaf fan. On a north window an adult plant merely survives.
40–60 % is enough. Wiping leaves helps — they are large and dusty. Constant damp around roots is not needed.
Summer 20–28 °C, winter not below 15 °C. A short cooler spell helps set flower stalks; frost and draught — no.
A large "bird of paradise" plant. Leaves torn along veins in wind are normal, not necessarily pests.
Water generously while growing; let the top layer dry; less in winter
Stable, fairly tight pot: in a huge one it blooms late
Do not break the leaf fan — each leaf feeds the plant for years
Flowering fertiliser every 2 weeks from spring to autumn
Indoor bloom happens on mature plants in a very bright spot
yucca: Yucca needs the brightest place and direct sun. In shade the trunk stretches, crown thins and new leaves emerge thin.

Summer 18–26 °C; winter cool 10–16 °C at the window is beneficial. In an overheated dark room in winter it weakens.
A false palm with a woody trunk. Soft trunk at the base is rot — stop watering at once.
Water after a good soil drying — fleshy roots rot in a full saucer
On a cool winter window, cut watering sharply

schefflera: Bright indirect light, with soft morning sun possible. Variegated forms need more light. Direct midday sun scorches umbrella leaflets; deep shade bares the stem.

Water after the top 2–3 cm dry; less in winter
Do not move abruptly: changing place causes shedding
A stretched top can be pinched for side branches

croton: Croton needs lots of bright light or red and yellow leaves green. Direct midday sun through glass can burn; morning sun helps.

Keep soil slightly moist — neither rock-hard nor swamp
Water with warm water and keep away from the window vent

fern-boston: Boston fern needs bright indirect light without direct sun. On north and east windows fronds are denser; on hot south they pale and dry.

ivy: Ivy needs bright indirect light. Variegated kinds green on the north side; direct summer sun dries leaves. Deep in the room vines stretch.

Water after light drying of the top layer; do not keep roots in water
Keep in the coolest bright place in the home

Check leaf undersides: mite loves ivy

echeveria: Echeveria needs direct sun or the rosette stretches and greens. On a south window leaves are tight with a pink flush.

Summer 18–28 °C by the glass. Winter better 10–16 °C with very rare watering. Wet cold below 8 °C is deadly.
Stone rose. A stretched stem with sparse leaves is lack of sun, not the variety.
Water at the root or in the saucer when soil is fully dry
Do not wet leaves or leave water in the rosette
Nearly mineral mix, pot with holes
Remove lower dry leaves so rot does not hide under them
Leaf cuttings dry and lie on dry soil — pups form at the leaf base
jade: Jade plant needs lots of light and direct sun part of the day. In shade stems thin, leaves small and far apart.
Dry air 30–50 % suits. Misting is unnecessary; brush dust with dry or slightly damp cloth.
Summer 18–26 °C. Winter cool 12–16 °C helps set bloom and prevents a leggy crown. Below 8 °C leaves turn watery.
Money tree stores water in leaves. Wrinkled leaves mean time to water; soft transparent ones mean already overwatered.
Water after full soil drying; even less in winter
Heavy crown likes a stable clay pot and not-too-rich mix
Cut stretched branches in spring — the bush branches
Fallen fleshy leaves can root if the cut is dried
Toxic to pets: do not let cats chew leaves
kalanchoe: Kalanchoe needs bright sun. In shade it stretches and stops blooming. A flowering plant from the shop can sit on east or south window.
Dry air 30–50 % is normal. Wet leaves and water in axils rot quickly.
Comfort is 16–26 °C. To rebloom, autumn needs long dark nights and cool around 16–18 °C.
A flowering succulent. In shops it is often overwatered: first step at home is to dry the soil, not water "on the shelf schedule".
Water when soil is dry; do not soak leaves and flowers
Cut spent umbels — neater and sooner new ones
After bloom give more light and less water
For repeat buds in autumn, 14 hours darkness daily for several weeks
pilea: Pilea needs bright indirect light. Direct midday sun scorches round leaves; shade stretches petioles and the plant leans one way.
40–60 % is enough. Dry air dries edges, but constant spray on leaves spots — pebble tray is better.
Cool 16–24 °C suits better than heat. Above 27 °C by a radiator leaves curl.
Chinese money plant with round leaves. A crooked stem usually means light from one side too long.
Water after the top 2 cm dry; less in winter
Rotate the pot weekly so "pancakes" do not face one way
Pups at the base can be potted when they have their own stem
Cut a stretched stem and root the top
Feed once a month at half strength in the growing season
rubber-plant: Rubber plant needs bright indirect light. Variegated kinds need more or white edges green. Direct midday sun spots the gloss.
40–60 % is normal. Large leaves must be wiped: dust dulls pattern and blocks breathing.
A steady 16–26 °C. Cold draught and below 13 °C cause spots and leaf drop.
Rubber tree forgives missed watering better than swamp. One lower leaf per season is growth; mass drop is cold or a move.
Water after the top few centimetres dry and empty the saucer
Wipe leaves with a damp cloth weekly
In spring you can cut the top — lower buds wake below
Feed every 2 weeks in the growing season
Milky sap irritates skin and stains floors — lay paper when pruning
palm-areca: Areca palm needs bright indirect light. Direct midday sun dries feathery fronds; deep shade makes them sparse and pale.
It likes 50–70 %. Dry air is the main cause of brown tips. Winter humidifier beats frequent fertiliser.
Warm 18–26 °C. Below 15 °C and draught blacken tips and stop growth.
A clumping palm without one trunk. Brown tips on an otherwise green frond usually mean dry air or hard water.
Keep soil evenly slightly moist, no puddle in the liner
Do not cut green fronds "for symmetry" — the palm grows them slowly
Trim only fully brown dry fronds at the trunk
Palm fertiliser every 2–3 weeks in spring and summer
Brown tips can be trimmed, but fix air and watering cause
citrus: Lemon and other citrus need direct sun, ideally south window. In shade they drop leaves and do not bloom. Winter almost always needs grow lights.
They like 50–70 %. Dry air and radiators cause leaf and bud drop. Pebble tray and shower help.
Summer 18–26 °C with airflow. Winter better 14–18 °C in light than +25 in a dark room. Sharp heat change from balcony causes leaf drop.
Indoor citrus needs more light than water. Winter leaf drop in a warm dark room is classic — fix with cool and a lamp.
Water when the top 2–3 cm dry, dechlorinated and not icy
Do not dry until leaves curl and do not keep saucer full
Citrus feed regularly in growth season; less in winter
Hand-pollinate flowers with a soft brush if no insects
Check leaf undersides: scale and mite are frequent guests
geranium: Pelargonium needs direct sun several hours a day. In shade it stretches and barely flowers. South and west windows are its place.
Slightly dry air 40–60 % beats a humid greenhouse. Do not mist flowers and dense leaves — grey mould appears.
Comfort is 16–25 °C. Winter cool 12–16 °C in light and sparse water helps. Heat without ventilation stops bloom.
Room geranium blooms from light and a slightly tight pot. Yellow lower leaves often mean overwatering, not hunger.
Water when soil is dry; do not wet leaves
Remove faded umbels with the flower stalk
Pinch tops so the bush is not one stick
Flowering fertiliser every 2 weeks from spring to autumn
Cuttings root easily: dry the cut and plant in slightly moist soil
spathiphyllum-mini: Mini peace lily is fine with soft diffused light and partial shade. Direct sun bleaches compact leaves; too dark a corner denies white spathes.
50–70 %, like the large relative. A small pot dries faster, but dry air still dries tips.
A steady 18–25 °C without draught. Below 15 °C leaf edges blacken.
Same crop as regular peace lily, only in a smaller soil volume. Watch watering more often than on a large plant.
Water when the top layer is dry: a small root ball dries faster
Drooping leaves recover the same day with water — do not wilt often
A snug pot helps bloom; a huge one only grows leaves
Weak feed every 2–3 weeks in season
Cut spent spathes at the base
oxalis: Oxalis needs bright indirect light. In sun triangular leaves keep purple colour; in shade they green and petioles stretch. Harsh noon is best softened.
Ordinary 40–60 % suits. Misting is optional; flowers spot from droplets.
Cool 15–24 °C prolongs a neat look. In heat and after a long season it may drop leaves and sleep — that is rest, not death.
Purple shamrock folds leaves at night and may go fully dormant. New leaves after dry rest are normal, not a miracle.
Water when the top layer is dry; almost none in dormancy
If all foliage collapsed and dried, rest the pot cool several weeks, then water again
Bulbs quickly fill the pot — divide when repotting
At night and on cloudy days it folds leaves — normal
Feed every 2–3 weeks while leaves are present
asparagus-fern: Asparagus fern needs bright indirect light. Direct midday sun yellows needle-like cladodes; deep shade bares thin stems.
It likes 50–70 %. Dry air makes the "foliage" shed. Shower and humidifier help more than daily heavy watering.
Comfort is 16–24 °C. Heat by a radiator and cold below 12 °C cause mass yellowing.
Not a fern but asparagus with root tubers. Shedding "needles" with live roots regrows if you restore light and humid air.
Keep soil slightly moist, not wet: tubers store water, swamp rots them
Cut yellowed branches at the base — new ones sprout from rhizome
Do not place above a radiator
Feed every 2 weeks in spring and summer
Berries if they appear are not edible — not for pets or children
